title: Project 3: Simulating Playoff Series Length
text:
In this project, I will simulate playoff series between two teams and see how sensitive the outcome is to how favored a team is, how long the series is, and home-field advantage. I will write a function that plays out a series game by game, with the games decided by Team A’s win probability. I will use map() variants to run the series thousands of times across different values in the parameters. At the end I will show how often Team A wins based on the different parameters.


Code
library(tidyverse)
set.seed(4747)

title: Project 3: Simulating Playoff Series Length
Project 3: Simulating Playoff Series Length
section: How series length changes the outcome
text:
How series length changes the outcome
I will turn off hfa and vary Team A’s p from 0.3 to 0.7 for each series length, and using map2_dbl(), run the simulation with every combination.


Code
p_values <- seq(0.3, 0.7, by = 0.05)
game_values <- c(1, 3, 5, 7)

length_sims <- tibble(
  p = rep(p_values, times = length(game_values)),
  games = rep(game_values, each = length(p_values))
) |>
  mutate(win_prob = map2_dbl(p, games, win_prob))

ggplot(length_sims, aes(x = p, y = win_prob, color = factor(games))) + 
  geom_line() + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") + 
  labs(title = "Probability Team A wins the series, by series length",
       x = "Team As single game win probability",
       y = "Probability Team A wins the series",
       color = "Best of (games)")









Every one of the curves passes through right around 0.5. This shows that if teams are evenly matched, both teams have even chances of winning no matter how long the series is. The further away from 0.5, the longer series give the better team a higher chance of winning. However, the effect is smaller then one may expect. A team that has a 55% chance of winning every game only wins the best of 7 series around 60% of the time.

title: Project 3: Simulating Playoff Series Length
text:
How home-field advantage matters
Next, we will put two evenly matched teams against each other, so any the only difference in p for the two teams will come from home-field advantage. I will vary the advantage from 0 to 0.15 for all the of the different length of the series. I will do this using pmap_dbl(), because there will be three changing inputs.


Code
hfa_values <- seq(0, 0.15, by = 0.015)

hfa_sims <- tibble(
  p = 0.5,
  games = rep(game_values, each = length(hfa_values)),
  hfa = rep(hfa_values, times = length(game_values))
) |>
  mutate(win_prob = pmap_dbl(list(p, games, hfa), win_prob))

ggplot(hfa_sims, aes(x = hfa, y = win_prob, color = factor(games))) + 
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Effect of Home-Field Advantage on Evenly Matched Teams",
    x = "Home-field advantage effect on p",
    y = "Probability team with HFA wins",
    color = "Best of (games)"
  )









As expected, having no hfa effect at all, all 4 different series length are scattered very closely around a 0.5 win probability. As the hfa grows, Team A’s chances rise, but by varying amounts based on the series length. In a best of 1, Team A gets the most benefit because they get the only home game, which is why as the effect grows, their probability soars way higher then the rest of the series, being close to a .1 higher probability then the best of 3, the one the hfa had the second highest effect on. The longer the series, the lower the effect of hfa had on the series outcome. There is a point for the best of 7 series where the hfa increases p by 0.09, where Team A only has a 0.5 chance of winning the series. It is even lower then when the hfa is 0 for the best of 7 series. This all shows that hfa has more effect on short series.

title: Project 3: Simulating Playoff Series Length
text:
Conclusion
I wrote a function that simulates a playoff series game by game, and used map_lgl(), map2_dbl(), pmap_dbl() to estimate series win probabilities across different team strengths, series lengths, and effects of home-field advantage. Longer series do slightly favor the better team, while series between closely matched teams are mostly 50/50 at any length. Home-field advantage gives the higher ranked team a large advantage in short series, but only a small advantage in a best of 7. These results suggest that leagues that have longer series usually have the best team win more often, while leagues that have shorter series usually favor a teams ranking and home-field advantage rather then the strength of the team.

fide_ratings_september <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2025/2025-09-23/fide_ratings_september.csv')

fide_ratings_september |>
  filter(title == "GM") |>
  count(fed, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = fct_reorder(fed, n))) + 
  geom_col() + 
  geom_text(aes(label = n), hjust = 1.3) +
  labs(
    x = "# of Grandmasters",
    y = "Country",
    title = "Countries with most Grandmasters"

Germany, the USA, and India are the countries with the most chess Grandmasters, having 77, 75, and 67, respectively. After the top 4 countries, which includes those named and Russia, there is a fairly steep drop off from 63 to 51 Grandmasters, which is Ukraine. Out of the top 10, there are 7 European countries, with the USA, India, and Israel being the only non-European countries. Numbers 5-10 are relatively close together, with each country only having a couple less Grandmasters then the one before it.

ufc_fights <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2026/2026-07-07/ufc_fights.csv')

Rows: 8736 Columns: 15
── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Delimiter: ","
chr  (13): fight_url, event_name, location, f1_name, f1_result, f2_name, f2_...
dbl   (1): round
date  (1): date

ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.



finish_by_year <- ufc_fights |>
  mutate(
    year = year(date),
    finish = if_else(str_detect(method, "KO"), "KO/TKO",
             if_else(str_detect(method, "Submission"), "Submission",
             if_else(str_detect(method, "Decision"), "Decision",
                     "Other")))
  ) |>
  count(year, finish) |>
  group_by(year) |>
  mutate(prop = n / sum(n)) |>
  ungroup()


finish_by_year |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = prop, color = finish)) + 
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.67) +
  geom_point() + 
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Proportion of fights",
    color = "Method",
    title = "Method of UFC fight finishes over time"
  )








In the first years of the UFC, decisions were very rare, and most fights ended by a KO/TKO or a submission. In the very initial years submissions were by far the most common method of finish. As the UFC heads into the late 1990s and the 2000s, you can see a clear trend of more and more fights ending in decision. All methods of finishes besides those labeled other fluctuate heavily by year throughout the 2000s, but the overall trend shows an increase in decisions and a decrease in KO/TKOS. Once you reach 2010, the trend of method of finishes become much more stable around the proportions that we have today, which is around half of fights ending in a decision, around 32% ending in a KO or TKO, and around 18% ending in submission. Throughout all years of the UFC fights ending in “other” ways, like disqualifications and no contests have remained incredibly rare, at a rate of around 1%.
